brief.head: Andheri to Arkansas
brief.text: A sale from Andheri to Bandra trou­bles no­body, Amit Varma said. Why should it mat­ter if the buyer sits in Arkansas? Every trade is two in­di­vid­u­als both gain­ing. {018-C09}

brief.head: South of the Vindhyas
brief.text: Warming will hit hard­est above the Vindhyas, Ajay Shah said. Families should be able to sell up and move south, but frozen land mar­kets keep them hug­ging the land. {018-C12}

brief.head: Spare the middleman
brief.text: Anger at mid­dle­men is easy pop­ulism, Ajay Shah warned. Traders work­ing within the state’s rules are not the vil­lains: “all that’s going on here is a lack of free­dom.” {018-C16}

brief.head: Harder than code
brief.text: Ajay Shah would nei­ther ban gene edit­ing nor rush it. Editing DNA, he said, is “a wee bit harder than edit­ing com­puter code”, and code goes wrong. {018-C17}

brief.head: The choke point
brief.text: India’s farm con­trols came from an ear­lier generation’s agri­cul­tural eco­nom­ics, Ajay Shah said. “What is wrong in India is the lack of ideas, is the lack of knowl­edge.” {018-C18}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on what ails Indian farming
lead.head: The state is the pest

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 18

body: Tomatoes in India had lately swung be­tween 200 ru­pees a kilo and two ru­pees, Ajay Shah said. People fly­ing in from abroad were asked to fill the rest of their bags with them. {018-R05}

For Shah and Amit Varma, the tomato was a way into a larger ques­tion: what is wrong with Indian agri­cul­ture? One prob­lem at a time, they kept ar­riv­ing at the same an­swer. The state is at the heart of it, and farm­ers are de­nied free­doms city peo­ple take for granted.
## Prices that ra­tion

Shah began with how prices work. If 90 units of toma­toes reach the mar­ket in­stead of 100, the price has to rise until enough buy­ers walk away. “So the price sys­tem should be un­der­stood as a ra­tioning mech­a­nism,” he said. {018-C01}
Staples such as wheat and rice, bought with­out a glance at the price, need huge swings to close a small gap. Avocados, a lux­ury, need only a small rise.

Paul Samuelson’s cob­web model adds the boom and bust: a high price makes ev­ery­one plant, and the glut crashes the price. But the model needs farm­ers to sow by look­ing back­ward, in­puts that are fixed and no way to store food, Shah said.
A swing from two ru­pees to 200, he said, is pe­cu­liar to India. Elsewhere, fu­tures mar­kets, stor­age, do­mes­tic trade and in­ter­na­tional trade keep food mar­kets calm.
## Penned in by law

India has hob­bled every one of those four. Farmers must sell at their local Agricultural Produce Market Committee, a state-made monop­sony. In one old study Varma re­called, farm­ers got two ru­pees for toma­toes that con­sumers bought for twenty. {018-C06}

Trade bans keep farm­ers below world prices, which the farmer leader Sharad Joshi called a neg­a­tive sub­sidy. City slick­ers think farm­ers live off hand­outs. In net terms, Varma said, they are pay­ing.
Holdings of one or two acres are “fun­da­men­tally sub­scale”, Shah said, and they breed near-feudal de­pen­dence on one local lender and buyer.
Land law locks the trap. Farmland can be sold only to an­other farmer, for farm­ing, so its price stays low and its own­ers can nei­ther exit nor bor­row against it.

In 1991 the rest of the econ­omy was lib­er­alised and agri­cul­ture was not, Varma said. Between 50 and 60 per cent of Indians are es­ti­mated to de­pend on farm­ing, which pro­duces 14 per cent of GDP.

Minimum sup­port prices bent what India grows. When ce­re­als got them, farm­ers left pulses, the main pro­tein for those who do not eat an­i­mals, and the state ended up feed­ing the di­a­betes epi­demic. {018-C14}
## The farm­ers who fought back
Varma’s hero was Joshi, who came home in 1977 from work in Bern and with the UN, bought a farm near Pune and built the Shetkari Sanghatana. Lakhs came to its ral­lies.
In 2002, boll­worms wrecked cot­ton across Gujarat, ex­cept on farms that had planted banned BT cot­ton bought on the black mar­ket. The gov­ern­ment or­dered the sur­viv­ing crop de­stroyed.
Joshi’s farm­ers stood on the fields and said “over our dead bod­ies”. The ban was lifted, and in time, Varma said, over 90 per cent of India’s cot­ton was BT. {#ninety}
“It was farm­ers who de­cided even if the gov­ern­ment has banned it, we have to save our­selves,” Varma said.
Joshi later spent years in the Rajya Sabha, where, Varma said, no­body cared for his ideas. His speeches there are col­lected as *Talking to an Empty Room*, a title that breaks Varma’s heart.

second.label: Agricultural markets
second.head: The columnists’ APMC
second.deck: Amit Varma imagines his own trade run like a farmers’ market committee

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the CPMC for columnists

body: Farmers must sell at their local Agricultural Produce Market Committee, their only legal buyer. To show what that means, Amit Varma imag­ined a ‘CPMC’ for colum­nists: he and Ajay Shah could legally sell their col­umns to it alone. {018-S04}

They would get per­haps a tenth of their present pay, he said, buy­ers would pay a crazy amount, and com­mit­tee pol­i­tics would rule. No city dweller would ac­cept buy­ing gro­ceries from one place at twenty times the price. {#grocery}

Yet elites in com­fort­able city lives, Varma said, an­swer re­form with “farm­ers will get ex­ploited”, though the re­cent farm bills left APMCs in place and only added a choice. It is, he said, “in­cred­i­bly con­de­scend­ing to farm­ers”.

quote.text: I hope you’re the best paid colum­nist in India, but per­haps not.

third.head: A thirsty land ships water

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the water India exports

body: Rice and sug­ar­cane are ex­tremely thirsty crops, and India ex­ports both. Exporting them, Amit Varma said, amounts to ex­port­ing water, which makes India one of the world’s big­gest ex­porters of water. {018-C15}
He cred­ited the shift in per­spec­tive to Ashok Gulati, the great agri­cul­tural econ­o­mist, who pointed to rice and sug­ar­cane as his ex­am­ples.

This hap­pens in a coun­try with droughts and chronic short­ages, he said, be­cause bad in­cen­tives make thirsty crops at­trac­tive. Punjab, rel­a­tively arid, grows rice any­way: there is a min­i­mum sup­port price for it, and free elec­tric­ity lets farm­ers pump the ground­wa­ter. {#electricity}
Varma called it a great con­cep­tual shift. “To think that we are ac­tu­ally one of the world’s big­gest ex­porters of water just blows my mind,” he said.

p2.deck: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah take Indian agriculture apart, one shackle at a time

box.title: The farmer who led farmers
box.text: Sharad Joshi’s *Down to Earth* col­lects the col­umns of a man who, Amit Varma said, took the role of pub­lic in­tel­lec­tual se­ri­ously. For farm­ing seen by a farmer who led a great move­ment, he said, this is the book. {018-R01}

sections.label: The price system
sections.head: Two rupees, two hundred
sections.caption: the price as a rationing mechanism
body: Prices move until the toma­toes bought equal the toma­toes sold, Ajay Shah said, and the way they get there is cruel. With 90 units in­stead of 100, the price must climb until some buy­ers walk away: to puree, or to a pav bhaji with more beet­root and less tomato. {018-C01}
How far it climbs de­pends on how flex­i­ble peo­ple are. Wheat and rice need huge swings to close a small gap; av­o­ca­dos need only a nudge.

Paul Samuelson’s cob­web model de­scribes a farm sec­tor stuck in boom and bust. Farmers see 200 ru­pees, all plant toma­toes, and the price crashes to two, with truck­loads dumped on the high­way. But the cycle needs three de­ci­sions to go wrong: sow­ing by look­ing back­ward, in­puts that are fixed, and no stor­age. {018-C02}
## Four shock ab­sorbers

Healthy mar­kets, Shah said, have four an­swers. Futures mar­kets show ev­ery­one the ex­pected price at har­vest, a pub­lic good even for farm­ers who never trade. Storage, in­clud­ing pro­cess­ing into paste and puree, moves food into the fu­ture. Domestic trade car­ries plenty in Andhra Pradesh to a short­age in Maharashtra. And the world mar­ket is “a great buf­fer stock”. {018-C03}

India has hob­bled all four. The old Forward Markets Commission, he said, was mostly “a game of ban­ning stuff”, and mov­ing com­mod­ity fu­tures under SEBI, which he had ar­gued for, changed lit­tle. {#fmc}
~ Whenever a price rises, Shah said, some pol­i­cy­maker wants to shoot the mes­sen­ger and shut the fu­tures mar­ket.

quote.text: The price that the spec­u­la­tors make on the fu­tures mar­ket is a pub­lic good.

portraits.credit: Innovation & Business Architectures, Inc., CC BY 1.0

sections.label: Storage and trade
sections.head: Hoarders, or God’s own work?
sections.caption: storage and speculation
body: Farming and stor­age are dif­fer­ent skills, Ajay Shah said. The farmer knows the land up to the farm gate. The spec­u­la­tor fore­casts a short­age, buys cheap and puts his own money on the line to carry food into a fu­ture where it will push prices down. {018-C04}

“Just like the pop­ulists hate in­tel­lec­tu­als, the pop­ulists hate spec­u­la­tors,” he said. He blamed the many Bengali movies about hoard­ers for giv­ing stor­age a bad name, and Amit Varma, who is half Bengali, replied: “For the pur­pose of this episode, Ajay, I’m half Punjabi.” {018-J04}
## The in­sur­ance pre­mium

Running stor­age is dull in most years, Shah said. Then once in ten or twenty years, prices spike and the op­er­a­tor makes “like a ban­dit”. That wind­fall pays for decades of stand­ing ready; seize it, and no­body builds the ca­pac­ity. {018-C05}
Why, he asked, would any­one build vac­cine ca­pac­ity in India after the state stopped mak­ers charg­ing a de­cent price at the peak of the pan­demic?

Export bans do sim­i­lar harm. When the war in Ukraine raised world wheat prices, India banned ex­ports of wheat and rice, though farm­ers would have earned more abroad. Sharad Joshi called such losses a neg­a­tive sub­sidy. {018-C07}
~ The global mar­ket, Shah said, is the big­gest sta­biliser of food prices, and India switches it off at a whim with sud­den im­port and ex­port bans.

quote.text: But that once in 10 years, once in 20 years, you make like a ban­dit.

art.caption: Ajay Shah on storage and speculation

sections.label: The land
sections.head: Check out, never leave
sections.caption: farmland that can’t be sold freely
body: Agricultural land in India can be sold only to an­other farmer, for farm­ing. That keeps its price low, Amit Varma said, draw­ing on his con­ver­sa­tion with Shruti Rajagopalan. {018-R12}
Change the land-use cer­tifi­cate and the value can rise forty times, so a com­mon scam is to buy farm­land through con­nec­tions and have it re­clas­si­fied. {#forty}
Genuine farm­ers, mean­while, can­not sell at a fair value and leave. Varma bor­rowed a line from *Hotel California*: “you can check out but you can never leave.” {018-J09}
## Dead cap­i­tal

Nor can they bor­row against land whose value is held down. Varma called it dead cap­i­tal, the idea at the heart of Hernando de Soto’s *The Mystery of Capital*, one of the great­est books he has read. {018-R04} He sees the same in un­ti­tled slums, idle gov­ern­ment land and FSI lim­its.

Each gen­er­a­tion di­vides the hold­ings among its chil­dren until they are no longer vi­able. Varma tied the anger be­hind ag­i­ta­tions for reser­va­tions by Jats, Patidars and Marathas, all landown­ing castes, to that squeeze. {#quota}
~ After Ajay Shah’s warn­ing about cli­mate change, Varma of­fered what he called “prob­a­bly an in­ap­pro­pri­ate joke”: if the state won’t let land mar­kets be liq­uid, maybe cli­mate change will.

quote.text: But hey, guess what, man? You don’t re­ally own your farm.

portraits.caption: Hernando de Soto
portraits.credit: Institute for Liberty and Democracy, CC BY-SA 3.0

sections.label: The big picture
sections.head: The bus India missed
sections.caption: structural transformation
body: In 1991, Amit Varma said, the parts of the econ­omy that af­fect rich and mid­dle-class peo­ple were lib­er­alised. Agriculture was not. {#liberal}
By the com­mon es­ti­mate, 50 to 60 per cent of Indians de­pend on farm­ing, which pro­duces 14 per cent of GDP. In the US, he said, the fig­ure is be­tween four and eight per cent. {#us}

As coun­tries grow, Ajay Shah said, they make a struc­tural trans­for­ma­tion, out of agri­cul­ture and from vil­lages to cities. India, apart from one great episode of growth from 1991 to 2011, has had weak growth, and the mod­ern-sector jobs have not come. {018-C13}
## Counting the farm­ers

Shah quib­bled with the fig­ures, which de­pend on how a sur­vey asks. A farmer with one rain-fed crop may do farm work for four months and none for eight, and al­most ev­ery­one counted as a farmer earns in other ways too.
Ask who pri­mar­ily re­lies on agri­cul­ture for in­come, and CMIE’s house­hold sur­vey gives about 35 per cent. {018-R25} That is still, Varma noted, eight to nine times the US level.
~ Small plots also block mech­a­ni­sa­tion, Shah added, so more peo­ple are needed to work the same land. All these prob­lems, he said, are in­tri­cately in­ter­con­nected.

quote.text: Structural trans­for­ma­tion is the tran­si­tion of a prim­i­tive coun­try out of agri­cul­ture and from rural to urban.

sections.label: Support prices
sections.head: Cereal offenders
sections.caption: minimum support prices
body: Minimum sup­port prices, Amit Varma said, are a clas­sic good in­ten­tion gone wrong. Around the 1960s, be­fore the green rev­o­lu­tion, the state set out to guar­an­tee that farm­ers could sell their crop.
The guar­an­tee was often hol­low. His guest Barun Mitra once found that in one year, MSPs were promised for 24 com­modi­ties and paid for only six. {#msp24}

Worse, the prices cor­rupted in­cen­tives. When ce­re­als got MSPs, farm­ers moved out of pulses, and until twelve or thir­teen years ago India grew too few, the main pro­tein for any­one who does not eat an­i­mals. {#pulses}
Ajay Shah added the health bill. Pulses were left to the mar­ket and ce­re­als got the sub­sidy, just as the hosts’ episode on di­a­betes urged peo­ple to eat less ce­real. {018-C14}
## A dry state’s wet crop

Varma’s other ex­am­ple, he said, was crazy. An MSP for rice and free elec­tric­ity have rel­a­tively arid Punjab pump­ing ground­wa­ter for a crop it should not grow, and burn­ing the stub­ble that chokes Delhi. {018-S05}
Shah called it one of the world’s worst pol­icy in­ter­ven­tions.
~ Sugarcane, also water-intensive, is caught in the same bad in­cen­tives, Varma said, and India ex­ports both crops.

quote.text: And in­stead the gov­ern­ment is sub­si­dis­ing the ce­real and am­pli­fy­ing the Indian di­a­betes epi­demic.

What we need is a new breed of thinkers who will build the par­a­digm, who will build the lit­er­a­ture, who will build the knowl­edge, who will change the cli­mate of opin­ion, who will change the con­sen­sus.

p3.title: Field reports
p3.deck: Seeds, smoke and a farmer-leader: the episode’s stories, and what each teaches

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the civil disobedience fought for a seed
stories.head: Satyagraha for a better seed
body: In the 1990s, Amit Varma said, a cri­sis was brew­ing in Indian cot­ton. Bollworms were de­stroy­ing the crop. Farmers fought back with pes­ti­cide, then more pes­ti­cide, in a race to the bot­tom, and crops still were not sur­viv­ing. {018-S01}

By then a ge­net­i­cally mod­i­fied va­ri­ety, BT cot­ton, had be­come avail­able across the world, and boll­worms did not at­tack it. The Indian gov­ern­ment, in­vok­ing the pre­cau­tion­ary prin­ci­ple, banned it, along with every ge­net­i­cally mod­i­fied or­gan­ism in agri­cul­ture and food.

A group of farm­ers in Gujarat got the seed any­way, from the black mar­ket as far as Varma re­mem­bered, and planted it. Then came 2002, when crops failed all across Gujarat, ex­cept on the BT farms. {#seminal}
“So guess what the gov­ern­ment did?” Varma said. “The gov­ern­ment said, Hey, that’s il­le­gal. We’re going to de­stroy those crops.” {#illegal}

Sharad Joshi’s Shetkari Sanghatana gath­ered farm­ers from Maharashtra and else­where and marched to Gujarat. They stood on those farms and said: over our dead bod­ies. Then they marched to Delhi with bales of cot­ton, and Varma’s friend Barun Mitra spoke at a fa­mous press con­fer­ence.

To the credit of the Vajpayee gov­ern­ment, Varma said, it saw sense and lifted the ban. {#vajpayee} When he last checked, about five years ago, over 90 per cent of India’s cot­ton was BT. India had be­come the big­gest pro­ducer and ex­porter of cot­ton in the world, pass­ing China.
~ Farmers are often talked about as if they have no agency, Varma said. Here they de­fied the state out of plain self-interest, and saved them­selves.
stories.why: Satyagraha is not only a word for the free­dom strug­gle. One of in­de­pen­dent India’s most in­spir­ing cam­paigns of civil dis­obe­di­ence, Varma ar­gued, was fought for the free­dom to plant a bet­ter seed.
stories.postscript: The se­quel: India stalled at two gen­er­a­tions of GM cot­ton, so farm­ers went back to the black mar­ket for HTBT seed. Some were ar­rested.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the BT cotton satyagraha

stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s answer to the lament for lost leaders
stories.head: From Bern to a farm in Ambethan
body: Independent India, peo­ple com­plain, had no great lead­ers. Sharad Joshi, Amit Varma said, was one of the great lead­ers of the cen­tury.

Born in 1935, Joshi taught eco­nom­ics, be­came a civil ser­vant and worked in in­for­mat­ics in Bern and with the UN. In 1977, in his for­ties, he bought 23 acres in Ambethan vil­lage, Pune dis­trict, and be­came a full-time farmer. {#acres}

He soon saw that ev­ery­thing was bro­ken, and traced it to state over­reach. Unlike the pes­simists, Varma said, he trusted every farmer to grasp it, and his Shetkari Sanghatana drew lakhs to its ral­lies. {018-S02}

~ Joshi also saw, as Mrinal Pande later wrote for Pragati, that be­hind every cri­sis in India lies a cri­sis of its women. His women’s wing, the Shetkari Mahila Aghadi, held a leg­endary rally of two lakh women farm­ers, and no men. {#twolakh}

quote.text: Sharad Joshi was not bound by such pes­simism. He said that no, this is some­thing every farmer should un­der­stand in­tu­itively.

stories.postscript: Later he spent years in the Rajya Sabha, where no­body lis­tened. His speeches there be­came *Talking to an Empty Room*. {018-R02}

stories.kicker: Amit Varma at a farmers’ gathering near Nashik
stories.head: Hayek without the books
body: About five or six years ago, Amit Varma’s friend Barun Mitra took him to a gath­er­ing near Nashik, where farmer lead­ers from across Maharashtra, Shetkari Sanghatana peo­ple among them, were meet­ing. {018-S03}
The trip pro­duced his only Hindi episode of *The Seen and the Unseen*, with Gunvant Patil, which he calls “a mas­ter­piece of il­lu­mi­na­tion”. It also taught him some­thing that moved him deeply.

His own be­liefs about lib­erty and the par­a­sitic state, he said, had come from books and frame­works, from a dis­tance. Farmer after farmer there held the same be­liefs, reached through lived ex­pe­ri­ence. “They had not read Hayek and Bastiat,” he said, “but they agreed with every word that Bastiat or Hayek would have writ­ten.” {#hayek}
~ That was an eye-opening mo­ment, Varma said. Grassroots pol­i­tics need not be all pop­ulism and the pol­i­tics of hand­outs.

quote.text: They’re ra­tio­nal human be­ings, they can see what is going wrong with them, they can ar­tic­u­late what is going wrong with them.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the farmers who had lived Hayek

stories.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah follow one subsidy downwind
stories.head: Rice in Punjab, smoke in Delhi
body: Punjab is rel­a­tively arid, Amit Varma said, with lim­ited ground­wa­ter, so it should not grow water-hungry rice. But the state guar­an­tees a min­i­mum sup­port price for rice and gives farm­ers free elec­tric­ity.

Farmers use the power to run bore wells and tube wells, pump­ing out more ground­wa­ter than the ecosys­tem can bear. {#electricity} After har­vest, the eas­i­est way to clear the stub­ble is to burn it, and the wind car­ries the smoke to Delhi.
What, he asked, is a Delhi chief min­is­ter to do, “when the prob­lem is caused by farm­ers in Punjab over which he has no ju­ris­dic­tion?” {018-S05}

~ Ajay Shah tot­ted up the bill. Each rupee raised in taxes costs so­ci­ety roughly three ru­pees in GDP, and sub­sidises rice and wheat that harm health, drain ground­wa­ter, strain the power sys­tem and fill the Hindi heartland’s air with par­tic­u­late mat­ter. {#taxes}
stories.why: One well-meant sub­sidy can spread into ground­wa­ter, diets and a cap­i­tal city’s air. The costs of a pol­icy often land far from where it was made, on peo­ple who had no say in it.
stories.postscript: In Tamil Nadu’s water cri­sis, Varma said, peo­ple were urged to take bucket baths while most water went to crops that shouldn’t have been grown.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Punjab’s paddy and Delhi’s smog

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 18. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Paul Samuelson (Innovation & Business Architectures, Inc., CC BY 1.0); Hernando de Soto (Institute for Liberty and Democracy, CC BY-SA 3.0).

shelf.title: Down to Earth
shelf.creator: Sharad Joshi
shelf.why: Joshi was a great thinker and politi­cian who also took the role of pub­lic in­tel­lec­tual se­ri­ously and worked hard to get his think­ing out.

shelf.title: Talking to an Empty Room
shelf.creator: Sharad Joshi
shelf.why: The title breaks Amit’s heart.

shelf.title: The Wizard and the Prophet
shelf.creator: Charles C Mann
shelf.why: It cov­ers the ten­sion be­tween the sci­en­tific and in­dus­trial rev­o­lu­tion in agri­cul­ture and con­cerns about sus­tain­abil­ity.

shelf.title: The Mystery of Capital
shelf.creator: Hernando De Soto
shelf.why: De Soto’s idea of ‘dead capital’: with­out prop­erty rights, un­ti­tled slum homes and re­stricted land are worth some­thing but can’t be bor­rowed against or in­vested, so the poor can’t turn what they own into cap­i­tal.

shelf.title: The Price of Onions
shelf.creator: Ashok Desai
shelf.why: Tomatoes swing­ing be­tween Rs 200 and Rs 2 a kg is the same story the book tells, with toma­toes in place of onions.

shelf.title: Why the Future Doesn’t Need Us
shelf.creator: Bill Joy
shelf.why: Joy wor­ried about micro-machines, nan­otech­nol­ogy and DNA edit­ing, and ar­gued that ev­ery­thing we know about how messy soft­ware is ap­plies to those fields too.

shelf.title: How I Reversed My Type 2 Diabetes (Episode 9)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Amit’s ac­count of re­vers­ing his di­a­betes through diet: eat less ce­real, avoid pro­cessed food, and treat ghee as a su­per­food and sugar as poi­son.

shelf.title: The Incredible Insights of Bastiat and Hayek (Episode 6)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Where the hosts first laid out how prices carry in­for­ma­tion and in­cen­tives that change the be­hav­iour of con­sumers and pro­duc­ers, and how tar­iffs re­dis­tribute wealth from the poor to the rich.

shelf.title: Why Freedom Matters (Episode 10)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Despite the title, an eco­nomic his­tory of India told through the lens of free­dom: the boom after 1869, Nehru’s Fabian so­cial­ism, the lost years from the 1962 war to the Emergency, and the open­ing-up that lifted mil­lions out of poverty.

shelf.title: Entry and Exit in Agriculture (Episode 1 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Pavan Srinath and Karthik Shashidhar
shelf.why: His guests ar­gued that small farm­ers are forced to mas­ter two skills, farm­ing and en­trepreneur­ship, when they might pre­fer to spe­cialise in one, and that tiny hold­ings make scale im­pos­si­ble.

shelf.title: Futures Markets in Agriculture (Episode 12 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Karthik Shashidhar
shelf.why: Amit once thought fu­tures were ar­cane fi­nance that didn’t con­cern or­di­nary peo­ple.

shelf.title: The Right to Property (Episode 26 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Shruti Rajagopalan
shelf.why: Rajagopalan ex­plains at length what this re­stric­tion leads to: de­pressed land prices, land-use-change scams, and farm­ers who can’t exit agri­cul­ture.

shelf.title: Our FSI Problem (Episode 11 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Alex Tabarrok
shelf.why: The source of Tabarrok’s line that Bombay re­claims the sea when it should be re­claim­ing the sky.

shelf.title: India’s Water Crisis (Episode 60 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Vishwanath S (zenrainman)
shelf.why: It cov­ers ground­wa­ter de­ple­tion in India, which is driven partly by bore wells and tube wells draw­ing ex­cess water be­cause of bad in­cen­tives.

shelf.title: The State of Our Farmers (Episode 86 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Gunvant Patil
shelf.why: A Hindi-language con­ver­sa­tion with Gunvant Patil on the con­di­tion of Indian farm­ers, which Amit calls ‘a mas­ter­piece of illumination’: farm­ers stat­ing free-market ideas drawn from lived ex­pe­ri­ence.

shelf.title: India’s Agriculture Crisis (Episode 140 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Barun Mitra and Kumar Anand
shelf.why: Barun Mitra and Kumar Anand on agri­cul­ture as a field where the state con­trols ev­ery­thing and farm­ers suf­fer, in­clud­ing the year MSPs were promised for 24 com­modi­ties but paid for only six.

shelf.title: The Tragedy of Our Farm Bills (Episode 211 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay and Amit on India’s farm bills, which would have kept APMCs but given farm­ers the choice to sell else­where, and on why farm re­form keeps stalling.

shelf.title: Farmers, Technology and Freedom of Choice: A Tale of Two Satyagrahas
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: The writ­ten ver­sion of the BT cot­ton satya­graha and what fol­lowed, in­clud­ing the adop­tion fig­ures he cites.

shelf.title: The Indian State Is the Greatest Enemy of the Indian Farmer
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s short piece ar­gu­ing that state over­reach, such as state-backed APMC mo­nop­o­lies that squeeze both farm­ers and con­sumers, is at the root of farmers’ mis­ery.

shelf.title: We Must Save Our Farmers
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: More of Amit’s writ­ten case for free­ing Indian agri­cul­ture.

shelf.title: Economic freedom in agriculture
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s writ­ten case for the episode’s con­clu­sion that what is wrong is a lack of free­dom, with the state block­ing vol­un­tary bar­gains.

shelf.title: India: An agricultural trade powerhouse
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s case for India’s stake in agri­cul­tural trade: the global mar­ket is the big­gest sta­biliser of food prices, which India’s on-off im­port and ex­port bans un­der­mine.

shelf.title: What happened to global food prices?
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Background on global food price move­ments and why Indian farm­ers should be free to sell abroad when world prices rise.

shelf.title: Climate change for practical people
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: It sets out Ajay’s view that the world will not hold back car­bon diox­ide emis­sions, so adap­ta­tion, in­clud­ing peo­ple mov­ing away from badly af­fected re­gions, be­comes es­sen­tial.

shelf.title: CMIE Consumer Pyramids Household Survey (CPHS) data
shelf.creator: CMIE
shelf.why: CMIE’s house­hold sur­vey (about 190,000 house­holds, three times a year, across some 100 ho­mo­ge­neous re­gions) makes India’s di­ver­sity mea­sur­able, from five­fold in­come gaps be­tween re­gions to how many house­holds re­ally live off farm­ing.

shelf.title: Rhyme and Reason
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit says this prob­a­bly made him the only pro­fes­sional lim­er­ick writer in the world.

laughs.text: Amit opens with a lim­er­ick called ‘Tomato’ about Ajay blush­ing at YouTube praise: ‘My good friend Ajay sat in his bed / read­ing YouTube com­ments in his head. / He was all aglow, like a tomato. / The ful­some praise made his cheeks go red.’

Ajay ad­mits that as a ‘cal­low im­ma­ture youth’ he pro­duced a lim­er­ick every ten min­utes, so the math­e­ma­ti­cian Meena Mahajan, a year se­nior at col­lege, nick­named him ‘Limya’ in the Maharashtrian style. Amit replies that he may be the world’s only pro­fes­sional lim­er­ick writer, hav­ing writ­ten a weekly lim­er­ick for the Sunday Times of India until it got too po­lit­i­cal.

Ajay calls stor­age ‘God’s own work’ and blames Bengalis: ‘be­cause there were so many Bengali movies around hoard­ers,’ stor­age got a bad name and the state out­lawed it. Amit, who is half Bengali, replies: ‘For the pur­pose of this episode, Ajay, I’m half Punjabi. We shall not refer to the other half... there is plenty to blame us Punjabis also for, as we shall find out.’ That sets up the later Punjab rice and stub­ble-burning story.
During the CPMC-for-columnists thought ex­per­i­ment, Amit tells Ajay: ‘I hope you’re the best paid colum­nist in India, but per­haps not.’

Sharad Joshi’s cou­plet, spo­ken by a farmer to a con­sumer: ‘Marte tum bhi ho, marte hum bhi hain.’ Amit trans­lates: ‘I die my friend and so do you. I sell my pro­duce cheap and die. You pay so much that you die too.’
